title: Given the roots of two binary trees, determine whether they are structurally identical and have the same values at every corresponding node.
shortTitle: Same Tree — check if two trees are identical

s1_definition.profdef: Same Tree checks whether two binary trees are identical in both shape and node values. It uses a parallel recursive traversal: at each step both nodes must be null together, or both non-null with equal values and recursively identical left and right subtrees. Any mismatch in structure or value short-circuits to false.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh has two copies of the bank's branch org chart, one from head office and one from the local branch, and he needs to verify they match exactly before an audit. He walks both charts in lockstep. At each position, either both charts have no one there, or both have the same person. If one chart has a manager where the other is empty, or the names differ, the charts are not the same and the audit fails immediately.
s1_definition.oneliner: Two trees are the same if both nodes are null, or both are non-null with equal values and identical left and right subtrees.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Same Tree checks whether two binary trees are identical in both shape and node values. It uses a parallel recursive traversal: at each step both nodes must be null together, or both non-null with equal values and recursively identical left and right subtrees. Any mismatch in structure or value short-circuits to false.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh has two copies of the bank's branch org chart, one from head office and one from the local branch, and he needs to verify they match exactly before an audit. He walks both charts in lockstep. At each position, either both charts have no one there, or both have the same person. If one chart has a manager where the other is empty, or the names differ, the charts are not the same and the audit fails immediately.

**One line to remember:** Two trees are the same if both nodes are null, or both are non-null with equal values and identical left and right subtrees.

sections.s2_technical:
The comparison is naturally recursive because two trees are identical exactly when their roots match and their corresponding subtrees are identical. You traverse both trees simultaneously, visiting corresponding positions together.

There are two base cases. First, if both nodes are null, this position matches, so return true. For example: `if (a == null && b == null) return true;`. Second, if exactly one is null, the structures differ, so return false. For example: `if (a == null || b == null) return false;`. The order matters: the both-null check must come before the one-null check.

The value check comes next: if the values differ at this position, the trees are not the same. For example: `if (a.getValue() != b.getValue()) return false;` or `.equals` for object values.

The recursive case requires both subtrees to match. For example: `return isSameTree(a.getLeft(), b.getLeft()) && isSameTree(a.getRight(), b.getRight());`. The logical and short-circuits, so a mismatch anywhere stops the comparison early.

The time complexity is linear in the number of nodes of the smaller tree, because the recursion stops as soon as a structural mismatch appears, and in the matching case it visits every node once. The space is proportional to the height due to the call stack. A senior nuance is that for object-valued trees you must use `.equals` rather than reference equality, and you should null-check values if they can be null, to avoid a NullPointerException during comparison.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, two independent systems maintain the branch approval hierarchy, and before an audit the compliance team must verify the two trees are byte-for-byte identical in both structure and the role at each position. A silent divergence could mean an unauthorized approver was inserted. This is exactly how Same Tree works — a lockstep comparison of both trees.

Problem 2 — The comparison must fail fast and point clearly to a match or mismatch, because audits run over many branches and performance matters. This is exactly why the recursion short-circuits on the first structural or value difference.

The mini-project builds a `RoleNode` class, a `HierarchyComparatorService` with a recursive `isSameTree` method and logging, and a runnable demo comparing two hierarchies that match and two that differ.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is two hierarchies, headOffice and branchMatch, both BranchManager with CreditOfficer on the left and RiskHead on the right.

Step 1: The service calls isSameTree on the two BranchManager roots. Neither is null, and both roles equal BranchManager, so it proceeds to compare left and right subtrees.

Step 2: It compares the left children, both CreditOfficer. Neither is null and roles match. Each CreditOfficer has null left and null right, so the recursive calls on both sides hit the both-null base case and return true. The left subtree matches.

Step 3: It compares the right children, both RiskHead. Same reasoning: roles match and both have null children, so this subtree matches.

Step 4: Both subtrees returned true, so the root comparison returns true and the service logs that the audit passed.

Step 5: For the second audit, headOffice versus branchDiff, the roots match and the left CreditOfficer matches, but the right children differ: RiskHead versus UnknownApprover. The role comparison fails, that subtree returns false, and the overall result short-circuits to false, logging that the audit failed.

```text
2026-10-26T17:40:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Hierarchy Audit (Same Tree)
2026-10-26T17:40:00Z [INFO] Hierarchies MATCH — audit passed
2026-10-26T17:40:00Z [SEVERE] Hierarchies DIFFER — audit FAILED, investigate
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Tree A root          Tree B root
  BranchManager   ==   BranchManager roles equal
     /     \              /     \
  Credit  Risk        Credit  Risk
    │       │            │       │
  compare left subtrees:  Credit==Credit (both leaves)
  compare right subtrees: Risk==Risk (both leaves)
    ▼
  true && true → SAME

  Mismatch case (B right = UnknownApprover):
  Risk != UnknownApprover → false → short-circuit → DIFFER
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Same Tree is a parallel recursion problem where I walk two trees in lockstep and verify that every corresponding position matches in both structure and value. The recursion has two base cases whose order matters: first, if both nodes are null, this position matches and I return true; second, if exactly one is null, the structures diverge and I return false. Only after passing both do I compare the values at the current position.

If the values match, I recurse into both left subtrees and both right subtrees, combining the results with a logical and. That and short-circuits, so the moment any position mismatches in shape or value, the comparison stops and the whole result collapses to false. This fail-fast behavior is exactly what you want when most comparisons either match fully or differ early.

The time complexity is linear in the number of nodes of the smaller tree, since a structural mismatch halts the recursion early and a full match visits every node once. The space is proportional to the tree height from the call stack. For object-valued nodes I always use the equals method rather than reference equality, and I use a null-safe comparison so that null values do not throw during the check.

In my project at National Bank of India, I used this in a hierarchy audit service. Two independent systems maintain the branch approval hierarchy, and before an audit we verify the two trees are identical in both shape and the role at each position. A silent divergence could mean an unauthorized approver was inserted, so the lockstep comparison fails fast on the first difference and raises a severe alert pointing the compliance team straight at the problem.
